description: Cross-driver regression corpus for hotstring expansion logic. Every vector must pass in both the AHK and Hammerspoon driver test suites without modification. 'vectors' covers single-trigger matching/arithmetic; 'collision_vectors' covers multi-trigger collision resolution (length > priority > first-registered).

field_semantics.terminator: The character typed after the trigger. The UNIT replays do not feed it — they match on the buffer tail as the last trigger character is typed, and take the only bit they need from terminator_consumed — but all three E2E runners DO inject it (tests/e2e/run_e2e.lua on macOS and Linux, run_e2e.ahk on Windows), so it is a real input at that layer. Changing it changes what the e2e harnesses type.
field_semantics.backspace_count: LOGICAL count: how many codepoints of already-typed text the expansion replaces (trigger length, plus 1 when terminator_consumed is true). It is NOT the number of backspace keystrokes a driver emits. macOS keeps the longest common prefix shared by trigger and replacement, so for 'btw' -> 'by the way' it emits 2 backspaces and types 'y the way' where Windows and Linux emit 3 and type the whole replacement; 6 of the 13 matched vectors below differ this way. All three drivers replace the same codepoints, which is what this field asserts and what makes it portable. A driver conforms by replacing that many codepoints, however few keystrokes it takes to do it.
field_semantics.is_case_sensitive: Registration shape, NOT comparison: true registers the trigger literally (no lower/Title/UPPER family). Matching still folds case unless is_case_sensitive_strict is also set. The name is inherited from the TOML schema and is the opposite of what it suggests.
field_semantics.is_case_sensitive_strict: Comparison: true means only the casing written in the TOML matches. This is the flag the domain spec calls is_case_sensitive.
field_semantics.driver_specific: Present when the vector's expected outcome depends on a constant that is deliberately per-driver. A driver whose constant differs must SKIP the vector rather than assert it, and say which constant. Absent means the vector is a cross-driver contract.
field_semantics.auto_expand: The AutoHotkey "*" flag under another name. true fires the moment the trigger's own last character is typed; false waits for a terminator, so "ya" does not fire inside "yaourt". Named here because reading it as a convenience toggle is what hid, for the corpus's whole life, that every vector in it was a star trigger and none covered the false case — the case macOS was getting wrong. A replay must drive the DISPATCH for this field: on macOS that is try_auto_expand, not would_fire, which is a pure buffer-tail predicate and does not decide it.

vectors.description: Exact trigger match expands to replacement.
Buffer that does not end with the trigger returns no match.

is_word trigger does not fire when preceded by a word character. Declares is_case_sensitive because its replacement is not lower-case: the cased FAMILY conforms the output to the typed trigger, and the lower variant is the LOWER-CASED replacement on Windows — so a family registration would silently discard the casing this vector is written with. Literal registration is what a real entry with an upper-case output uses, and it keeps the vector about the rule it names.

is_word trigger fires when it is the entire buffer (start-of-line). Declares is_case_sensitive because its replacement is not lower-case: the cased FAMILY conforms the output to the typed trigger, and the lower variant is the LOWER-CASED replacement on Windows — so a family registration would silently discard the casing this vector is written with. Literal registration is what a real entry with an upper-case output uses, and it keeps the vector about the rule it names.

is_word trigger fires when preceded by a space. Declares is_case_sensitive because its replacement is not lower-case: the cased FAMILY conforms the output to the typed trigger, and the lower variant is the LOWER-CASED replacement on Windows — so a family registration would silently discard the casing this vector is written with. Literal registration is what a real entry with an upper-case output uses, and it keeps the vector about the rule it names.

is_word trigger fires when preceded by punctuation. Declares is_case_sensitive because its replacement is not lower-case: the cased FAMILY conforms the output to the typed trigger, and the lower variant is the LOWER-CASED replacement on Windows — so a family registration would silently discard the casing this vector is written with. Literal registration is what a real entry with an upper-case output uses, and it keeps the vector about the rule it names.

is_case_sensitive_strict is the flag that makes the COMPARISON exact: a different casing must not fire. The corpus sets is_case_sensitive alongside it because all 1 302 shared entries that declare strict also declare it — see case_literal_folds for what the second flag does on its own.
A strict trigger fires on the casing written in the TOML, and its replacement is emitted verbatim.

backspace_count equals trigger length when terminator is not consumed. Declares is_case_sensitive because its replacement is not lower-case: the cased FAMILY conforms the output to the typed trigger, and the lower variant is the LOWER-CASED replacement on Windows — so a family registration would silently discard the casing this vector is written with. Literal registration is what a real entry with an upper-case output uses, and it keeps the vector about the rule it names.
backspace_count = trigger_length + 1 when terminator is consumed.
Buffer that is a strict prefix of the trigger does not match.
Trigger containing an apostrophe expands correctly.
Multi-word replacement is returned verbatim.
Empty buffer never produces a match.
Trigger containing a 2-byte UTF-8 character (é): backspace_count must equal codepoint count, not byte count.
Trigger with 3 multi-byte UTF-8 codepoints (àèù): backspace_count = 3 (codepoints), not 6 (bytes).

is_word trigger fires when preceded by a newline (\n is a word boundary). Declares is_case_sensitive because its replacement is not lower-case: the cased FAMILY conforms the output to the typed trigger, and the lower variant is the LOWER-CASED replacement on Windows — so a family registration would silently discard the casing this vector is written with. Literal registration is what a real entry with an upper-case output uses, and it keeps the vector about the rule it names.

is_word trigger fires when preceded by a tab (\t is a word boundary). Declares is_case_sensitive because its replacement is not lower-case: the cased FAMILY conforms the output to the typed trigger, and the lower variant is the LOWER-CASED replacement on Windows — so a family registration would silently discard the casing this vector is written with. Literal registration is what a real entry with an upper-case output uses, and it keeps the vector about the rule it names.

A trigger longer than the 256-codepoint rolling buffer can never match: the window cannot hold it in full. The engine states this in a comment and nothing exercised it. DRIVER-SPECIFIC: the cap is not shared — the Lua engine holds 256 codepoints and macOS holds 500 — so this vector's outcome is only defined for a driver whose window is 256. A replay on any other driver must skip it; the caps themselves are held by test-hotstring-buffer-cap-parity.cjs. Declares is_case_sensitive because its replacement is not lower-case: the cased FAMILY conforms the output to the typed trigger, and the lower variant is the LOWER-CASED replacement on Windows — so a family registration would silently discard the casing this vector is written with. Literal registration is what a real entry with an upper-case output uses, and it keeps the vector about the rule it names.

A trigger of exactly 256 codepoints still matches. Pins the boundary itself, not merely the far side of it — an off-by-one in the eviction loop would break this while leaving the 257 case passing. Declares is_case_sensitive because its replacement is not lower-case: the cased FAMILY conforms the output to the typed trigger, and the lower variant is the LOWER-CASED replacement on Windows — so a family registration would silently discard the casing this vector is written with. Literal registration is what a real entry with an upper-case output uses, and it keeps the vector about the rule it names.
A buffer far longer than the window still matches on its tail: eviction drops the OLDEST codepoints, so the most recent characters — the only ones a trigger can end on — survive.

The DEFAULT mode registers the cased family, so an all-caps buffer matches a lower-case trigger AND the replacement is conformed to the casing that was typed. Windows registers the three variants explicitly, macOS and Linux conform at fire time; the observable result is this one.

A Title-cased buffer yields a Title-cased replacement. This vector replaces one that asserted the opposite — that the matcher returns the replacement verbatim and case conformance is 'a driver-level concern'. It is not: Windows produces the conformed output from the registry and both Lua drivers now do the same, so a matcher that skipped it disagreed with every driver.
A casing that is neither lower, Title nor UPPER fires nothing: no variant is registered for it, and conforming would have to invent an output casing. All three drivers decline.

is_case_sensitive WITHOUT strict selects the REGISTRATION shape, not the comparison: the trigger is registered literally — no lower/Title/UPPER family — and still matches any casing, emitting its replacement verbatim. 592 shared entries have this shape, all acronym autocorrections like "adn" -> "ADN": the literal registration exists so the family cannot generate "Adn" -> "Adn", and the fold is what lets a capitalised "Adn" correct at all. Reading the flag as "compare exactly" — which its name invites — makes every one of them silently stop firing on any casing but the one written.

Case folding does not bypass the word-boundary rule: a mid-word occurrence stays blocked even when the case differs from the trigger. Declares is_case_sensitive because its replacement is not lower-case: the cased FAMILY conforms the output to the typed trigger, and the lower variant is the LOWER-CASED replacement on Windows — so a family registration would silently discard the casing this vector is written with. Literal registration is what a real entry with an upper-case output uses, and it keeps the vector about the rule it names.

A trigger ending in the magic key matches when that key is typed. backspace_count is 3, not 5: the star is ONE codepoint even though it is three UTF-8 bytes, which is the distinction backspace_count exists to make.

A trigger that begins with the magic key matches at the tail of a longer buffer, so the star is an ordinary codepoint to the matcher rather than a mode switch. Declares is_case_sensitive because its replacement is not lower-case: the cased FAMILY conforms the output to the typed trigger, and the lower variant is the LOWER-CASED replacement on Windows — so a family registration would silently discard the casing this vector is written with. Literal registration is what a real entry with an upper-case output uses, and it keeps the vector about the rule it names.

is_word_char treats EVERY non-ASCII codepoint as a word character — deliberate, so accented letters behave like letters — and the magic key inherits that. A word-boundary trigger typed straight after the star is therefore blocked. The rule was stated only in a comment; this pins it, so changing is_word_char to consult Unicode categories cannot alter it silently. Declares is_case_sensitive because its replacement is not lower-case: the cased FAMILY conforms the output to the typed trigger, and the lower variant is the LOWER-CASED replacement on Windows — so a family registration would silently discard the casing this vector is written with. Literal registration is what a real entry with an upper-case output uses, and it keeps the vector about the rule it names.

A trigger WITHOUT auto_expand must not fire when its own last character is typed. This is the case the shared engine comment calls the whole point of the field — "ya" inside "yaourt" — and until 2026-08-04 no vector covered it: all 29 carried auto_expand = true. macOS had no gate at any level and expanded on the spot, rewriting the word as the user typed it; Linux and Windows gated it by two unrelated mechanisms. Three implementations, one invariant, nothing shared holding them to it. THE `terminator` HERE IS DELIBERATELY NOT ONE: "o" is the next letter of "yaourt". The vector first shipped with the field absent, and every e2e runner defaults a missing terminator to a space — so all three typed "ya" then SPACE, the non-auto trigger fired exactly as it is supposed to on a terminator, and the vector failed on two drivers while claiming to describe the opposite. Naming the character that actually follows makes the same sentence true at both layers: the unit replays still stop at the trigger's last character, and the e2e runners now finish the word instead of ending it.

The contrast. Same trigger, same buffer — only auto_expand differs, and the outcome flips. Without it the vector above passes on any driver that never matches anything, which is the shape a corpus takes when it stops testing and starts agreeing with itself.

A mapping whose replacement equals what was typed must NOT fire. macOS guards this at expander.lua would_fire ("if eff_plain == typed then …") because it once shipped without it: the expansion consumed the triggering keystroke while injecting nothing, so the character vanished from the screen — the dropped-char bug named in try_auto_expand own comment. The shared core has no such guard, and this vector is what tells us whether that matters.

An is_word trigger whose FIRST character is a space is word-gated like every other one: preceded by a letter, it does not fire. macOS used to exempt these — any trigger whose first BYTE was space, NBSP, NNBSP or ';' skipped the boundary check entirely — while AutoHotkey exempted nothing and the shared core exempted nothing either. Three shipped entries fired on macOS and nowhere else because of it. Measured 2026-08-04: the exemption's stated reason, the comma-layer ';e' -> 'Je', has no carrier at all — ZERO shipped triggers begin with ';'. The exemption was removed and the three entries' is_word flag, which had only ever subtracted behaviour, came off with it.

The positive control for the vector above. Without it, a driver that refuses every separator-prefixed trigger — the opposite defect — would satisfy the negative case and look correct. Preceded by a full stop, which opens no word, the same mapping fires.

collision_vectors.description: Two equal-length triggers (same string, two sources) collide; the higher priority wins regardless of registration order. The high-priority mapping is registered LAST here. Case-sensitive triggers isolate the tie-break from case-variant generation. Tie-break order is length > priority > first-registered, identical in the AHK engine and the Hammerspoon registry.
Same collision as above but the high-priority mapping is registered FIRST; the outcome must not depend on registration order.
Equal length AND equal priority falls back to first-registered (seq), the pre-priority default preserved on both drivers.
Length stays primary: a longer trigger wins even against a shorter, far-higher-priority one.

The personal source default (50) outranks the common source default (10) for an identical trigger — the user-facing 'my personal hotstring always wins' contract. Personal is registered FIRST, as at startup; priority, not load order, decides. This is the case the macOS group-aware dedup fix restored.

The personal tier wins even when the common entry is registered FIRST. personal_tier_beats_common_tier registers them the other way round, so a driver that resolved collisions by registration order alone would pass it — and did. Both orders are needed for the tier itself to be load-bearing.
When the buffer does not end with any registered trigger, nothing fires even though competing mappings exist.

is_word is a FILTER, not a tie-break. Mid-word the word-bounded mapping is blocked by the boundary rule, so the unbounded one wins whichever order they were registered in — verified by replaying both orders. At a word boundary BOTH are eligible and the engine falls back to first-registered, which is order-dependent and deliberately not asserted: such a vector would pass or fail on registration order rather than on the rule.
